Schenectady.wildlife_intro:
Schenectady keeps our crew busy with Norway rats and pigeons downtown, raccoons along the river, and squirrels and bats in the older housing. Mohawk River  gives wildlife food, water, and cover within a short run of almost every roof in town, and the housing does the rest — once an animal finds a soft soffit, an uncapped chimney, or a gap at the roofline, it treats the house as part of its territory.

The year has a rhythm in Schenectady. Fall pushes squirrels, raccoons, and rodents indoors ahead of winter; spring brings denning mothers looking for chimneys and attic corners; summer is when bat colonies are most visible in older homes and when young animals start ranging on their own. Most Schenectady jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

faqs.q: Can you get pigeons and starlings out of my Rotterdam building?
faqs.a: Yes — European starlings, house sparrows, and unbanded pigeons are the birds that can be legally removed in New York, and they are exactly what nests in Rotterdam's vents, soffits, and sign structures. Our crew removes the birds and nesting, then covers vents and seals roost ledges so the flock does not return the following week.

Rotterdam.wildlife_intro:
Rotterdam sprawls west and south of Schenectady along the Mohawk, a working suburb of postwar streets, rail lines, and big commercial strips. Its bird work sets it apart: unbanded pigeons and European starlings fill the vents, signs, and warehouse eaves along the commercial corridors, while the residential streets behind them get the standard raccoon and squirrel attic calls. The canal-era hamlet of Rotterdam Junction, out along the river, adds older housing and river-edge skunks.

Starling pressure peaks in Rotterdam in late winter, when flocks test every louvered vent on the older homes, and pigeon roosting is a year-round commercial problem. Residential calls follow the usual Mohawk Valley rhythm — fall squirrels, spring raccoon litters, summer skunks under porches. Our crew handles Rotterdam jobs as two checklists: bird proofing with vent covers and roost deterrents where the birds are, and a full roofline inspection for the mammal entries that often share the same building.

faqs.q: Why do squirrels keep coming back to Niskayuna attics?
faqs.a: Niskayuna's oak canopy feeds and shelters a dense gray squirrel population, and any home with overhanging limbs is a short jump from a roof. Removing one squirrel without sealing every soffit gap and cutting back the bridge limbs just opens the attic to the next one — our crew pairs removal with full sealing and tells you honestly which limbs are doing the damage.

Niskayuna.wildlife_intro:
Niskayuna is Schenectady County's leafy, affluent suburb along the Mohawk, where large older homes, deep lots, and a heavy oak canopy produce a particular kind of call: gray squirrels in quantity, raccoons in big chimneys, and big brown bat colonies in the eaves and attics of the town's substantial pre-war and colonial housing. The Lock 7 riverfront and the bike-path corridor keep a wooded edge running behind whole neighborhoods.

Mature canopy is the whole story here — branches overhang roofs on street after street, so squirrel entries recur unless the sealing is thorough and the worst limbs are cut back. Summer bat colonies in Niskayuna's older homes are often large, and fall brings the second squirrel push as acorns drop. Our crew inspects these bigger homes bay by bay, removes the animals, and seals every dormer, valley, and eave junction, because a large roof has more junctions than a small one and the quote should say so honestly.

faqs.q: What should I expect to pay for wildlife removal in Glenville?
faqs.a: A Glenville quote can mean attic sealing in the suburbs or burrow screening on a rural lot, and those are different jobs with different costs. We inspect the property, identify the animal and its entries, and quote the specific removal and proofing your place needs, in writing.

faqs.q: Are groundhogs really a problem in Glenville, or just a nuisance?
faqs.a: Both — Glenville's open lots, pasture edges, and sunny banks are prime woodchuck ground, and a burrow system under a shed or along a foundation undermines soil and channels water against the structure. Our crew removes the groundhogs and screens the denning voids; leaving an open burrow system behind invites the next animal to move into ready-made shelter.

Glenville.wildlife_intro:
Glenville occupies the north bank of the Mohawk across from Schenectady, mixing the suburban streets behind Scotia with genuinely rural roads running out toward Charlton. Groundhogs are the headline call on the town's open lots and small farms, skunks den under outbuildings, and squirrels and raccoons cover the suburban end. The Alplaus hamlet along Alplaus Kill adds creek-bottom habitat that keeps opossums and raccoons moving through backyards.

Glenville's seasons are farm seasons at one end and suburb seasons at the other: groundhogs dig from March thaw, skunk kits appear under sheds in June, and the suburban streets get their squirrel rush in October. Our crew scopes Glenville properties by type — full roofline and foundation work on the houses, burrow and void screening on the rural lots — removes the animals, and seals what the inspection actually found rather than selling a standard package.

faqs.q: What does it cost to get an animal out of my Scotia attic?
faqs.a: Scotia's older homes are compact, which keeps many jobs straightforward, but layered additions and shared tree canopy can add entries the first look misses. We inspect the whole house, additions included, and quote removal and sealing in writing before work starts — no figures guessed over the phone.

faqs.q: Why are bats so common in Scotia's older homes?
faqs.a: The village's pre-war housing offers exactly what big brown bats want: warm eave gaps, louvered vents, and a short flight to the Mohawk River's insect hatches. Bat work here is exclusion only — one-way exits installed, every other gap sealed, timed around the maternity season as professional practice. Our crew identifies the entries at dusk watch when needed and quotes the full seal, not just the main hole.

Scotia.wildlife_intro:
Scotia is a compact, old-fashioned village on the Mohawk's north bank, facing Schenectady across the river, where nearly every street is lined with pre-war homes under big trees. Raccoons in chimneys and big brown bats in the eaves of the older housing are the village's signature calls, with squirrels working the canopy along Collins Park and the riverfront. The lots are small and the houses close, so one animal's route often crosses several roofs.

Village density changes the advice: a raccoon denning on one Scotia street is feeding across the whole block, and sealing one house while the neighbor's chimney stays open just moves the problem. Fall brings the bat colonies' last activity and the squirrel push together; spring is chimney season. Our crew inspects Scotia homes completely, removes the animals, and caps and seals the entries — and we will tell you plainly when a neighbor's open flue is part of your problem.
